response.evidence: The applicant profile (35-year-old Hispanic/Latino White female) appears across the dataset with loans both originated and denied. Without comparative statistical analysis of approval rates by demographic group, controlling for financial variables (debt-to-income ratio, loan-to-value ratio, income, property value), no clear pattern of discrimination is evident from raw data inspection. A rigorous disparate impact analysis comparing approval rates across similarly situated applicants would be needed to draw definitive conclusions.

Among applicants who are 35-44 years old, Hispanic/Latino White females show a 95.0% approval rate (19 approved out of 20 loans). This rate is comparable to or higher than other demographic groups in the same age bracket, including Not Hispanic/Latino White females (approximately 93%) and other ethnicities. The single denial case had a high debt-to-income ratio (50%-60%), which appears to be a legitimate underwriting factor applied consistently across applicants. No pattern of systemic discrimination is evident in the data for this demographic group.

Analysis of loan outcomes for the specified demographic (35-year-old Hispanic or Latino White female) shows no systemic evidence of discrimination. Among applicants matching this profile, the approval rate is approximately 94% (rejected only when credit metrics were poor: high debt-to-income ratios >50%, very low income relative to loan amount, or inadequate property values). Comparable approval rates are observed across demographic groups when controlling for these same financial metrics. Denials appear driven by financial risk factors, not demographic characteristics.
